subject: physics
title: Earth, Sun and Moon
key_idea: The Earth spins on its tilted axis once in about 24 hours, which gives day and night. It orbits the Sun once in about 365 days, which gives the seasons. The Moon orbits the Earth in about a month, which gives its phases.

blocks.text: The Earth turns on its axis. This section covers what that spin explains.

items: The Earth **rotates** on its axis once in approximately 24 hours.
The axis is an imaginary line through the North and South Poles. It is tilted.
At any moment, the half of the Earth facing the Sun has day and the other half has night.
As the Earth turns, a place moves from the daylight side to the dark side, so day and night repeat every 24 hours.
The Sun appears to rise in the east, move across the sky and set in the west.
This is only apparent motion. The Sun does not move round the Earth: the Earth spins.
The Earth rotates once in about 24 hours.
Rotation causes day and night and the Sun's apparent daily motion across the sky.

blocks.text: The Earth also orbits the Sun. This section covers why this gives seasons.

items: The Earth orbits the Sun once in approximately 365 days (one year).
The Earth's axis stays tilted in the same direction as it orbits.
So for part of the year the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, and for part of the year it is tilted away.

rows: Sun's rays hit the ground at
A steeper angle, so they are more concentrated
A shallower angle, so they are more spread out

items: The northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun in June, so it is summer there.
At the same time the southern hemisphere is tilted away, so it is winter there.
Countries far from the Equator show the biggest changes in temperature through the year.
The Earth orbits the Sun once in about 365 days.
The tilt of the axis and the orbit together cause the seasons.
In summer the Sun's rays hit at a steeper angle and daylight lasts longer.

blocks.text: The Moon orbits the Earth. This section covers why its shape seems to change.

items: The Moon orbits the Earth once in approximately **1 month**.
The Moon does not give out light. We see it because it reflects light from the Sun.
The Sun always lights half of the Moon.
As the Moon orbits, we see different amounts of the lit half. These are the **phases** of the Moon.
New Moon: the lit half faces away from us, so we see almost none of it.
Full Moon: the lit half faces us, so we see a full circle.
In between, we see a crescent or a half circle.
The cycle of phases repeats about every month.

blocks.text: An orbit is nearly a circle. This section covers how to find the speed of an object in orbit.

items.meaning: The time taken for one complete orbit.
The average distance from the centre of the orbit to the orbiting object.

blocks.label: Average orbital speed
where: v = average orbital speed, in m/s
r = average radius of the orbit, in m

items: In one orbit the object travels the circumference of a circle, 2πr, in a time T.
Convert the period to seconds first: 1 day = 24 × 60 × 60 s = 86 400 s.
Keep the radius in the unit you want in the speed: km gives km/s, m gives m/s.
